title: A nonzero comodule over a connected filtered coalgebra has a group-like coinvariant
statement:
Let $k$ be a field [def-weil-field]. Let $C$ be a $k$-vector space with $k$-linear maps $\Delta:C\to C\otimes_k C$ and $\epsilon:C\to k$ satisfying $(\Delta\otimes1_C)\Delta=(1_C\otimes\Delta)\Delta$ and $(\epsilon\otimes1_C)\Delta=(1_C\otimes\epsilon)\Delta=1_C$, under the canonical tensor identifications; tensor products are as in [def-weil-pbc-module-tensor-product]. Let $g\in C$ satisfy $\Delta(g)=g\otimes g$ and $\epsilon(g)=1$. Suppose $C$ has increasing $k$-linear subspaces $C_0\subseteq C_1\subseteq\cdots$ with $C_0=kg$, $\bigcup_{r\geq0}C_r=C$, and
$$\Delta(C_r)\subseteq\sum_{i=0}^r C_i\otimes_k C_{r-i}\quad(r\geq0),$$
where each tensor subspace means its image in $C\otimes_k C$. Let $V$ be any nonzero $k$-vector space with a $k$-linear map $c:V\to V\otimes_k C$ satisfying $(c\otimes1_C)c=(1_V\otimes\Delta)c$ and $(1_V\otimes\epsilon)c=1_V$. Then there exists $v\in V$ with $v\ne0$ and $c(v)=v\otimes g$. No algebra structure on $C$, cocommutativity, or finite-dimensionality of $C$ or $V$ is assumed.

source.place: Definition 14.4, equation (91), printed p.281; Theorem 14.5, proof of (c) implies (a), printed pp.281–282. This argument uses only the displayed filtration, the coalgebra and comodule identities, and the distinguished group-like element, not multiplication or the antipode.

proof.text: For $r\geq0$ put $T_r=\operatorname{im}(V\otimes_k C_r\to V\otimes_k C)$ and $V_r=c^{-1}(T_r)$. These are increasing subspaces. Every tensor is a finite sum of pure tensors by [def-weil-pbc-module-tensor-product]. For $v\in V$, write $c(v)=\sum_{j=1}^m v_j\otimes a_j$. Exhaustivity puts each $a_j$ in some $C_{r_j}$; taking the maximum of these finitely many indices (and $r=0$ for an empty sum) puts $v$ in $V_r$. Hence $\bigcup_r V_r=V$.

source.place: Theorem 14.5(c) implies (a), printed p.281, definition and exhaustivity of the subspaces V_r.

proof.text: Let $Q_r=C/C_r$, let $q_r:C\to Q_r$ be the quotient map, and put $d_r=(1_V\otimes q_r)c$. Apply [lem-weil-pbc-tensor-right-exact] to $C_r\to C\to Q_r\to0$, tensoring on the left with $V$. It gives $\ker(1_V\otimes q_r)=T_r$. Thus $\ker d_r=V_r$. In particular $V_r=0$ implies that $d_r$ is injective: $d_r(v)=d_r(w)$ gives $v-w\in\ker d_r=0$.

source.place: Theorem 14.5(c) implies (a), printed p.282, quotient-map injectivity; tensor kernel justification by Stacks Tag 00DF (algebra.tex, lemma-tensor-product-exact).

proof.text:
Suppose $V_r=0$. Apply [lem-sfb-vector-space-tensor-family-zero-detection] with the singleton family consisting of $d_r:V\to V\otimes_k Q_r$, and right factor $Q_r$. Step 2 verifies its zero-detection hypothesis, so $d_r\otimes1_{Q_r}$ is injective. Consequently $(d_r\otimes1_{Q_r})d_r$ is injective. On $v\in V_{r+1}$, coassociativity identifies its value with
$$(1_V\otimes q_r\otimes q_r)(1_V\otimes\Delta)c(v).$$
Indeed, both quotient factors applied to $(c\otimes1_C)c(v)=(1_V\otimes\Delta)c(v)$ give this formula. Since $c(v)\in T_{r+1}$, the filtration puts $(1_V\otimes\Delta)c(v)$ in the sum of the images of $V\otimes C_i\otimes C_{r+1-i}$ for $0\leq i\leq r+1$. For every such $i$, either $i\leq r$ or $r+1-i\leq r$; that factor is killed by $q_r$, using the increasing filtration. The displayed value is therefore zero. Injectivity forces $v=0$, proving $V_r=0\Rightarrow V_{r+1}=0$.

source.place: Theorem 14.5(c) implies (a), printed p.282, the displayed induction implication and the two quotient factors.

proof.text: If $V_0=0$, induction on $r$ gives $V_r=0$ for all $r$: the base is the supposition, and the step is precisely step 3. Exhaustivity from step 1 then gives $V=0$, contrary to the hypothesis. Thus choose $0\ne v\in V_0$.

source.place: Theorem 14.5(c) implies (a), printed p.282, V_0=0 implies V=0.

proof.text: Because $C_0=kg$, a finite pure-tensor expression for an element of $T_0$ has the form $\sum_j v_j\otimes(\lambda_jg)=(\sum_j\lambda_jv_j)\otimes g$. Apply this to $c(v)$ to obtain $c(v)=w\otimes g$. The comodule counit identity and $\epsilon(g)=1$ give $v=(1_V\otimes\epsilon)c(v)=\epsilon(g)w=w$. Hence $c(v)=v\otimes g$, with $v\ne0$ as required.

source.place: Theorem 14.5(c) implies (a), printed p.282, first paragraph, applying the counit to a vector in V_0.

proof_origin.place: Theorem 14.5, proof of (c) implies (a), printed pp.281–282; with g replacing the Hopf unit, and the implicit tensor kernel and injectivity facts supplied by the cited nodes.
